title: Interferometry reveals spin-singlet fractional quantum Hall edges in graphene
authors: R. Ayache, K. Kim, M. Kuiri, Q. Benichou, H. Chakraborti, L. Pugliese, K. Watanabe, T. Taniguchi, H. -S. Sim, P. Roulleau
abstract: The edge modes of spin-singlet fractional quantum Hall (FQH) phases are manifestations of multicomponent topological order and SU(2) spin symmetry. An archetype is the spin-unpolarized state at $ν$=2/3, whose edge is expected to host spatially coexisting yet counter-propagating charge and neutral spin modes. Despite efforts, its edge properties, including spin coherence and spin-charge separation, have remained elusive owing to the difficulty of resolving spins in FQH edge transport. Here, we develop a spin-sensitive probe of graphene FQH edges by using a p-n junction to interface a target FQH state with a probe integer quantum Hall (QH) state of opposite polarity. An Aharonov-Bohm (AB) interferometer forms along the interface, when the target and probe edge channels carry the same spin. We identify the spin-unpolarized and polarized edges of the $ν$=2/3 states at lower and higher magnetic fields, respectively, through spin-dependent interference. A novel multiparticle AB interference between two electrons of opposite spin emerges from spin-charge separation and recombination on the unpolarized edge, featuring a spin swap. Our results establish edge transport as a probe of spin-singlet topological orders, with implications for parafermion platforms in graphene-superconductor hybrids.
summary: This work reports on using Aharonov-Bohm interferometry in graphene to directly probe the spin structure of fractional quantum Hall edge states. By coupling the target FQH edge to a spin-polarized probe, the researchers distinguish between spin-unpolarized and spin-polarized regimes of the $\nu=2/3$ state. This establishes edge transport as a key diagnostic tool for understanding spin-singlet topological orders.
main_problem: The study aims to develop a spin-sensitive probe to characterize the spin-singlet topological order present in fractional quantum Hall (FQH) edge states, particularly the $\nu=2/3$ state.
main_result: The authors successfully identified the spin-unpolarized and spin-polarized regimes of the $\nu=2/3$ edge state using Aharonov-Bohm interferometry, confirming the existence of spin-charge separation effects.
method: The primary method involves using a p-n junction to couple a target FQH edge state to a probe integer QH state, forming an Aharonov-Bohm interferometer whose interference pattern is spin-dependent.
model_or_system: The system is graphene exhibiting FQH edge states. The theoretical analysis models the edge using boson fields and investigates the transition between $SU(2)$-symmetric (unpolarized) and broken symmetry (polarized) regimes.
key_observables: Aharonov-Bohm oscillation visibility, frequency components ($f_{nm}$), and the transition point in transmission ($\delta T$) between spin-unpolarized and spin-polarized states.
important_parameters: Filling factors ($\nu=2/3$), magnetic field ($B$), and the ratio of spin-up/spin-down coupling strengths.
main_assumptions: The interference pattern is governed by spin matching between the probe and target channels; the theoretical analysis assumes specific velocity orderings and negligible intra-channel interactions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate device schematics, AB oscillation measurements showing single/dual MZI frequencies, and theoretical models detailing the spin-charge separation and fractionalization into downstream/upstream components.
paper_structure: The paper moves from experimental demonstration of spin-sensitive probing via AB interferometry in graphene to theoretical analysis of the resulting interference patterns, confirming spin-charge separation and fractionalization across different symmetry regimes.
why_interesting: The ability to probe spin degrees of freedom in topological edge states using interferometry provides a powerful experimental tool for studying exotic quantum phases, which is highly relevant to understanding strongly correlated electron systems.
